source_steps.text: Fix arbitrary x∈R^n and t>0. H001 makes the coordinate sums finite, and H002 permits componentwise product rules and equality of mixed derivatives. H004 gives u·u=1. Differentiating in time yields 2u·u_t=0, hence u·u_t=0. Differentiating once more yields 2|u_t|²+2u·u_tt=0, hence u·u_tt=-|u_t|². For each spatial coordinate j=1,…,n, two differentiations of the same unit constraint yield 2|∂_{x_j}u|²+2u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=0, hence u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=-|∂_{x_j}u|². These are routine product-rule calculations on the open domain R^n×(0,∞).

Choose the pointwise scalar a from H005. By F001, u_t·(u_tt-Δ_xu)=a(u_t·u)=0. Dotting u_tt-Δ_xu=a u with u and using H004 and F001 gives a=u·u_tt-∑_{j=1}^n u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=∑_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u|²-|u_t|². Substitution gives the stated explicit wave-map equation. The same calculation applies to any scalar satisfying the pointwise normality equation, so it also proves the assertion about every such scalar. No derivative or regular selection of a was used. Eliminate this pointwise witness and universally quantify the arbitrary x,t to obtain all asserted tangency identities and the explicit wave-map equation.

Fix t0>0 and J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. Since 0<t0/2<3t0/2, H006 gives a compact C with u(x,r)=q for x∉C, r∈J. H001 supplies the positive finite spatial dimension. A compact subset of Euclidean space is bounded; choosing a strict larger coordinate bound, there exists R>0 with C⊂(-R,R)^n. This standard compactness consequence also covers an empty C (any positive R works).

Choose R as in F001 and set Q=[-R,R]^n. Its Lebesgue measure is (2R)^n<∞, by the product formula for a coordinate box. Compact C is closed; hence (R^n\C)×int(J) is open. On this open set u is the constant vector q: H003 supplies that q is fixed, and H006 supplies the equality. By H002, every positive-order derivative of u therefore vanishes there. In particular e,e_t and the scalar functions u_t·u_tt, ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t, u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u, u_t·∂_{x_j}u and ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u) for every spatial index j vanish there. Smoothness, finite sums and products also imply their continuity (indeed smoothness). For a fixed r∈int(J), each scalar function is bounded on compact Q and zero off C⊂Q. Its absolute value is consequently bounded by a finite constant times the measurable indicator 1_Q; continuous sections are measurable, and this bound has finite integral because μ(Q)=(2R)^n. Thus all listed sections are absolutely integrable. The same boundedness argument on Q×K for any compact subinterval K⊂int(J) proves all the asserted uniform bounds.

The properties in F002 hold for the witnesses C,R chosen above. In particular t0∈int(J), so e(·,t0) is integrable. Package their existence, with the displayed formulas J=[t0/2,3t0/2] and Q=[-R,R]^n, and quantify over arbitrary t0>0. This proves all the asserted support and boundedness properties, including integrability at every positive time. The choices of C and R remain existential for each time window.

Fix t0>0, put J=[t0/2,3t0/2], and choose C,R from N002 for this t0; put Q=[-R,R]^n. N002 gives finiteness of the spatial energy integrals for every positive time, so the guarded definition of E is available. H001 gives the finite coordinate range. H002 gives the product rule and equality ∂_t∂_{x_j}u=∂_{x_j}u_t. Hence pointwise on the full domain, e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2∑_{j=1}^n ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t. By N002 these terms are spatially integrable at all times in int(J).

Set η=t0/4>0. Then [t0-η,t0+η]⊂int(J). By F001 and N002, e_t is continuous on the compact Q×[t0-η,t0+η], so its absolute value has a finite nonnegative bound. Consequently there exists B≥0 with |e_t(x,r)|≤B on that box. The compactness and boundedness facts used here are the standard extreme-value property for continuous real functions on a compact finite-dimensional box.

Choose B from F002. Fix x∈R^n and a real h, and temporarily assume L1: 0<|h|<η. For x∈Q, apply M002 to the real function r↦e(x,r) on the interval with endpoints min(t0,t0+h) and max(t0,t0+h), and derivative r↦e_t(x,r). Both endpoints and the full interval lie in [t0-η,t0+η]. F001 supplies differentiability and continuity there, and F002 bounds the intermediate derivative. The theorem's slope is (e(x,t0+h)-e(x,t0))/h also when h<0, because reversing both differences changes neither quotient. Thus its absolute value is at most B. If x∉Q, N002 makes both densities zero and gives the same estimate with right side zero. Discharge L1 and quantify x,h: for all x and all 0<|h|<η, |(e(x,t0+h)-e(x,t0))/h|≤B 1_Q(x). The right side is integrable by μ(Q)=(2R)^n<∞, from N002.

Fix an arbitrary real sequence hseq and temporarily assume L2: 0<|hseq(k)|<η for every k and hseq(k)→0. Define Fseq(k)(y)=(e(y,t0+hseq(k))-e(y,t0))/hseq(k). These are continuous real spatial functions, hence μ-almost everywhere strongly measurable. By F003 they are dominated pointwise by B 1_Q, which is integrable. Smoothness in F001 gives pointwise convergence Fseq(k)(y)→e_t(y,t0). Apply M001 with spatial Lebesgue measure μ and real codomain: ∫Fseq(k) dμ→∫e_t(y,t0) dμ. For each k, the two densities are integrable by N002; integral linearity and scalar multiplication identify ∫Fseq(k) dμ=(E(t0+hseq(k))-E(t0))/hseq(k). Thus the energy difference quotients converge to ∫e_t(y,t0) dμ along this sequence.

Discharge L2 in F004 and quantify the arbitrary sequence. Any sequence of nonzero real increments tending to zero eventually satisfies |h|<η, so discarding its finite initial part yields the same limit. The sequential criterion for limits in R now gives the full two-sided difference-quotient limit at zero. Explicitly, if that limit failed, a fixed positive error could be attained by nonzero increments arbitrarily close to zero; choosing one at distance less than min(η,1/(k+1)) for each k would contradict the just-proved sequence limit. Thus E is differentiable at t0 and E'(t0)=∫ e_t(x,t0) dx. Substitute F001 and use finite linearity of the integral; every summand is absolutely integrable by N002. This yields E'(t0)=2∫u_t·u_tt dx+2∑_{j=1}^n ∫∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t dx, at time t0. The pointwise formula, finiteness, and arbitrary choice of t0 prove all asserted differentiation identities and finiteness clauses.

Fix t0>0 and j∈{1,…,n}; H001 supplies n≥1. Choose C,R from N002 for J=[t0/2,3t0/2], and set Q=[-R,R]^n. Define g(x)=u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0). By H002 it is smooth. Its derivative, by the product rule, is ∂_{x_j}g=∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u+u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u at time t0. By N002, both summands, g and its derivative are integrable and vanish off C. Since C⊂int(Q), the complement of C is an open neighborhood of the boundary of Q, and g vanishes there. In particular the two j-coordinate face values are zero.

Use the coordinate insertion I_j(y,z), with coordinate j equal to z and remaining coordinates given by y. Fix arbitrary y∈[-R,R]^(n-1), and define fline(z)=g(I_j(y,z)), dline(z)=∂_{x_j}g(I_j(y,z)). By F001 and the coordinate chain rule, fline is smooth, its derivative is dline, and both endpoint values fline(-R),fline(R) are zero. The continuous derivative dline is bounded and integrable on [-R,R]. Apply M003 with real codomain and a=-R,b=R: ∫_{-R..R}dline(z) dz=fline(R)-fline(-R)=0. Endpoints are null for one-dimensional Lebesgue measure, so the same holds for the integral over [-R,R]. Since y was arbitrary, the integral in coordinate j of ∂_{x_j}g is zero for every choice of remaining box coordinates.

Set v(y,z)=∂_{x_j}g(I_j(y,z)). Split Q into its remaining n-1 coordinates and coordinate j, with their restricted Lebesgue measures. This is the same measure as μ restricted to Q under I_j: on every coordinate subrectangle both give the product of its side lengths, and these rectangles determine the finite measures; the coordinate reordering merely reorders these factors. Both restricted measures are finite, hence s-finite. The function v is continuous and bounded on the compact product box, so it is integrable for that finite product measure. Apply M004 to v with the remaining coordinates as the outer variable and coordinate j as the inner variable. This gives ∫_Q ∂_{x_j}g dx=∫_{[-R,R]^(n-1)}(∫_{[-R,R]}∂_{x_j}g(I_j(y,z)) dz) dy=0 by F002. For n=1 the remaining-coordinate space is R^0, a singleton with its zero-dimensional Lebesgue measure of mass one, so the identical formula reduces to the one-dimensional integral; no exceptional empty-coordinate case is omitted.

By F001 all terms vanish off C⊂Q, so F003 gives ∫_{R^n}∂_{x_j}g dx=0. The product identity in F001 and integral linearity, justified by absolute integrability of both summands, give 0=∫_{R^n} ∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0) dx+∫_{R^n}u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(x,t0) dx. Symmetry of the dot product and rearrangement yield ∫∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t dx=-∫u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx, with all terms at time t0. Quantify over the arbitrary t0 and j to conclude the asserted integration-by-parts formula and its finiteness assertions.

Fix arbitrary t0>0. H001 gives finitely many spatial coordinates, and H002 supplies the derivative notation. N002 proves e(·,t0) integrable and thereby makes the guarded definition of E available. N003 proves differentiability of E at t0 and the absolutely finite identity E'(t0)=2∫u_t·u_tt dx+2∑_{j=1}^n∫∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t dx. Apply N004 at t0 for each of the finitely many spatial indices to replace each second integral by -∫u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx.

By the definition Δ_xu=∑_{j=1}^n∂_{x_jx_j}u and finite linearity of these integrable terms, F001 becomes E'(t0)=2∫_{R^n}u_t(x,t0)·(u_tt(x,t0)-Δ_xu(x,t0)) dx. N001 states that this integrand is zero pointwise, hence E'(t0)=0. Since t0 was arbitrary, E is differentiable on (0,∞) and has zero derivative at every positive time. N002 already supplies integrability for every such time.

For completeness take any 0<a0<b0. F002 gives differentiability, hence continuity, of E at all points of [a0,b0], and derivative zero on (a0,b0). Apply M002 with f equal to E on positive times, derivative function zero there, and endpoints a0,b0 (extend f arbitrarily to nonpositive arguments). It yields (E(b0)-E(a0))/(b0-a0)=0; since b0-a0>0, E(b0)=E(a0). Equality is automatic for coincident times, and for reversed positive times interchange their roles. Therefore E is constant on (0,∞). Together with F002 and the definition of E this proves the complete conclusion with coefficient one on both squared norms and without any time-zero assertion.

1: # Conservation of energy for a sphere-valued wave map
2: 
3: ## Original exercise
4: 
5: Lawrence C. Evans, *Partial Differential Equations*, second edition,
6: Graduate Studies in Mathematics 19, AMS, 2010, section 12.6, exercise 14,
7: printed page 694. The preceding exercise 13 defines the sphere-valued
8: wave map. ISBN: 978-0-8218-4974-3.
9: 
10: > 14. Prove that if \(\mathbf u\) is a wave map into the unit sphere,
11: > with compact support in space, we have conservation of energy:
12: > \[
13: > \frac{d}{dt}\int_{\mathbb R^n}
14: >       |\mathbf u_t|^2+|D\mathbf u|^2\,dx=0.
15: > \]
16: 
17: ## Fixed interpretation and complete target
18: 
19: A sphere-valued map cannot vanish outside a compact set. As approved by
20: the user on 2026-10-23, interpret spatial compact support as compact support
21: of a perturbation from a **fixed unit vector**, locally uniformly in time.
22: This is a disclosed nontrivial interpretation, not a claimed author-issued
23: correction.
24: 
25: Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
26: \(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
27: Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:
28: 
29: 1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
30: 2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
31:    \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
32:    \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
33:    assumed.
34: 3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
35:    \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
36:    \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).
37: 
38: With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define
39: 
40: \[
41: e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
42: \qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
43: \]
44: 
45: The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
46: \(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
47: Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
48: and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.
49: 
50: ## Fixed natural-language proof
51: 
52: ### 1. Tangency and the wave-map equation
53: 
54: Differentiate \(u\cdot u=1\) in time. The product rule gives
55: \(2u\cdot u_t=0\), so
56: 
57: \[
58: u\cdot u_t=0,\qquad
59: u_t\cdot(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu)=a(u_t\cdot u)=0.          \tag{1}
60: \]
61: 
62: No derivative of \(a\) is needed. The familiar explicit equation also
63: follows from the assumptions: twice differentiating the unit constraint
64: gives \(u\cdot u_{tt}=-|u_t|^2\) and
65: \(u\cdot\partial_{x_jx_j}u=-|\partial_{x_j}u|^2\).
66: Dotting the normality equation with \(u\), using \(|u|^2=1\), yields
67: \(a=\sum_j|\partial_{x_j}u|^2-|u_t|^2\). This is a consequence,
68: not an additional PDE assumption.
69: 
70: ### 2. Common compact support and integrability
71: 
72: Fix \(t_0>0\), put \(J=[t_0/2,3t_0/2]\), and choose its compact
73: spatial set \(C\) from assumption 3. Since \(C\) is bounded, choose
74: \(R>0\) with \(C\subset(-R,R)^n\) and set \(Q=[-R,R]^n\).
75: The box has finite Lebesgue measure \((2R)^n\).
76: 
77: On the open set \((\mathbb R^n\setminus C)\times\operatorname{int}J\),
78: the map equals the constant \(q\), so all its positive-order
79: derivatives vanish. At interior times, \(e\), \(e_t\), and the
80: derivative products used below consequently vanish outside \(C\).
81: They are continuous by smoothness; their spatial sections are measurable,
82: bounded on \(Q\), and supported there. Their absolute integrals are
83: bounded by a finite constant times \(|Q|\). This proves integrability
84: of \(e(\cdot,t_0)\) and of all later terms. Since \(t_0\) was arbitrary,
85: the energy is a finite, well-defined integral at every positive time.
86: 
87: ### 3. Differentiate the energy integral
88: 
89: The product rule and equality of mixed derivatives give
90: 
91: \[
92: e_t=2u_t\cdot u_{tt}
93:    +2\sum_{j=1}^n\partial_{x_j}u\cdot\partial_{x_j}u_t.           \tag{2}
94: \]
95: 
96: Choose \(\eta>0\) so that
97: \([t_0-\eta,t_0+\eta]\subset\operatorname{int}J\).
98: Continuity of (2) on the compact box
99: \(Q\times[t_0-\eta,t_0+\eta]\) gives a finite bound \(|e_t|\leq B\).
100: For \(0<|h|<\eta\), the one-variable mean value theorem at fixed
101: \(x\) therefore gives
102: 
103: \[
104: \left|\frac{e(x,t_0+h)-e(x,t_0)}h\right|
105: \leq B\mathbf1_Q(x).
106: \]
107: 
108: Outside \(Q\), both densities vanish, so the bound holds throughout
109: \(\mathbb R^n\). The right side is integrable. The difference
110: quotients converge pointwise to \(e_t(x,t_0)\). Dominated convergence
111: and linearity for these integrable functions now prove
112: 
113: \[
114: E'(t_0)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e_t(x,t_0)\,dx.            \tag{3}
115: \]
116: 
117: This establishes differentiability of the actual finite integral.
118: 
119: ### 4. Integration by parts and cancellation
120: 
121: For each spatial index \(j\), at time \(t_0\) put
122: \(g_j(x)=u_t(x,t_0)\cdot\partial_{x_j}u(x,t_0)\).
123: It is smooth and vanishes on a neighborhood of the boundary of \(Q\),
124: because \(C\subset\operatorname{int}Q\). The product rule gives
125: 
126: \[
127: \partial_{x_j}g_j
128: =\partial_{x_j}u_t\cdot\partial_{x_j}u
129:  +u_t\cdot\partial_{x_jx_j}u.
130: \]
131: 
132: Integrate first over \(x_j\in[-R,R]\) at fixed remaining coordinates.
133: The fundamental theorem of calculus gives zero because both endpoint
134: values of \(g_j\) are zero. Fubini applies on \(Q\) because the
135: derivative and its two summands are continuous and bounded on a
136: finite-measure box. Thus \(\int_Q\partial_{x_j}g_j=0\).
137: All these terms vanish outside \(Q\), so
138: 
139: \[
140: \int_{\mathbb R^n}\partial_{x_j}u\cdot\partial_{x_j}u_t\,dx
141: =-\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_t\cdot\partial_{x_jx_j}u\,dx.              \tag{4}
142: \]
143: 
144: Every integral is finite by step 2. Sum (4) over the finitely many
145: spatial indices and substitute (2) into (3):
146: 
147: \[
148: \begin{aligned}
149: E'(t_0)
150: &=2\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_t\cdot u_{tt}\,dx
151:  -2\sum_{j=1}^n\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_t\cdot\partial_{x_jx_j}u\,dx\\
152: &=2\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_t\cdot(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu)\,dx=0,
153: \end{aligned}
154: \]
155: 
156: by (1). This holds at every \(t_0>0\). Hence \(E\) is differentiable
157: with zero derivative on \((0,\infty)\), and is constant there by the
158: mean value theorem. This is conservation of energy with exactly the
159: normalization in the exercise.

A sphere-valued map cannot vanish outside a compact set. As approved by
the user on 2026-10-23, interpret spatial compact support as compact support
of a perturbation from a **fixed unit vector**, locally uniformly in time.
This is a disclosed nontrivial interpretation, not a claimed author-issued
correction.

Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
\(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:

1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
   \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
   \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
   assumed.
3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
   \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
   \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).

With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define

\[
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
\qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
\]

The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
\(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.
value.conclusion: For every t>0, e(·,t) is Lebesgue integrable on R^n. The finite energy E(t)=∫_{R^n} (|u_t(x,t)|²+∑_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u(x,t)|²) dx is differentiable on (0,∞) and E'(t)=0 for every t>0. In particular E is constant on (0,∞), with exactly this normalization; no assertion at time zero is made.

source_steps.text: Fix arbitrary x∈R^n and t>0. H001 makes the coordinate sums finite, and H002 permits componentwise product rules and equality of mixed derivatives. H004 gives u·u=1. Differentiating in time yields 2u·u_t=0, hence u·u_t=0. Differentiating once more yields 2|u_t|²+2u·u_tt=0, hence u·u_tt=-|u_t|². For each spatial coordinate j=1,…,n, two differentiations of the same unit constraint yield 2|∂_{x_j}u|²+2u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=0, hence u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=-|∂_{x_j}u|². These are routine product-rule calculations on the open domain R^n×(0,∞).

Choose the pointwise scalar a from H005. By F001, u_t·(u_tt-Δ_xu)=a(u_t·u)=0. Dotting u_tt-Δ_xu=a u with u and using H004 and F001 gives a=u·u_tt-∑_{j=1}^n u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=∑_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u|²-|u_t|². Substitution gives the stated explicit wave-map equation. The same calculation applies to any scalar satisfying the pointwise normality equation, so it also proves the assertion about every such scalar. No derivative or regular selection of a was used. Eliminate this pointwise witness and universally quantify the arbitrary x,t to obtain all asserted tangency identities and the explicit wave-map equation.

Fix t0>0 and J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. Since 0<t0/2<3t0/2, H006 gives a compact C with u(x,r)=q for x∉C, r∈J. H001 supplies the positive finite spatial dimension. A compact subset of Euclidean space is bounded; choosing a strict larger coordinate bound, there exists R>0 with C⊂(-R,R)^n. This standard compactness consequence also covers an empty C (any positive R works).

Choose R as in F001 and set Q=[-R,R]^n. Its Lebesgue measure is (2R)^n<∞, by the product formula for a coordinate box. Compact C is closed; hence (R^n\C)×int(J) is open. On this open set u is the constant vector q: H003 supplies that q is fixed, and H006 supplies the equality. By H002, every positive-order derivative of u therefore vanishes there. In particular e,e_t and the scalar functions u_t·u_tt, ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t, u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u, u_t·∂_{x_j}u and ∂_{x_j}(u_t·∂_{x_j}u) for every spatial index j vanish there. Smoothness, finite sums and products also imply their continuity (indeed smoothness). For a fixed r∈int(J), each scalar function is bounded on compact Q and zero off C⊂Q. Its absolute value is consequently bounded by a finite constant times the measurable indicator 1_Q; continuous sections are measurable, and this bound has finite integral because μ(Q)=(2R)^n. Thus all listed sections are absolutely integrable. The same boundedness argument on Q×K for any compact subinterval K⊂int(J) proves all the asserted uniform bounds.

The properties in F002 hold for the witnesses C,R chosen above. In particular t0∈int(J), so e(·,t0) is integrable. Package their existence, with the displayed formulas J=[t0/2,3t0/2] and Q=[-R,R]^n, and quantify over arbitrary t0>0. This proves all the asserted support and boundedness properties, including integrability at every positive time. The choices of C and R remain existential for each time window.

Fix t0>0, put J=[t0/2,3t0/2], and choose C,R from N002 for this t0; put Q=[-R,R]^n. N002 gives finiteness of the spatial energy integrals for every positive time, so the guarded definition of E is available. H001 gives the finite coordinate range. H002 gives the product rule and equality ∂_t∂_{x_j}u=∂_{x_j}u_t. Hence pointwise on the full domain, e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2∑_{j=1}^n ∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t. By N002 these terms are spatially integrable at all times in int(J).

Set η=t0/4>0. Then [t0-η,t0+η]⊂int(J). By F001 and N002, e_t is continuous on the compact Q×[t0-η,t0+η], so its absolute value has a finite nonnegative bound. Consequently there exists B≥0 with |e_t(x,r)|≤B on that box. The compactness and boundedness facts used here are the standard extreme-value property for continuous real functions on a compact finite-dimensional box.

Choose B from F002. Fix x∈R^n and a real h, and temporarily assume L1: 0<|h|<η. For x∈Q, apply M002 to the real function r↦e(x,r) on the interval with endpoints min(t0,t0+h) and max(t0,t0+h), and derivative r↦e_t(x,r). Both endpoints and the full interval lie in [t0-η,t0+η]. F001 supplies differentiability and continuity there, and F002 bounds the intermediate derivative. The theorem's slope is (e(x,t0+h)-e(x,t0))/h also when h<0, because reversing both differences changes neither quotient. Thus its absolute value is at most B. If x∉Q, N002 makes both densities zero and gives the same estimate with right side zero. Discharge L1 and quantify x,h: for all x and all 0<|h|<η, |(e(x,t0+h)-e(x,t0))/h|≤B 1_Q(x). The right side is integrable by μ(Q)=(2R)^n<∞, from N002.

Fix an arbitrary real sequence hseq and temporarily assume L2: 0<|hseq(k)|<η for every k and hseq(k)→0. Define Fseq(k)(y)=(e(y,t0+hseq(k))-e(y,t0))/hseq(k). These are continuous real spatial functions, hence μ-almost everywhere strongly measurable. By F003 they are dominated pointwise by B 1_Q, which is integrable. Smoothness in F001 gives pointwise convergence Fseq(k)(y)→e_t(y,t0). Apply M001 with spatial Lebesgue measure μ and real codomain: ∫Fseq(k) dμ→∫e_t(y,t0) dμ. For each k, the two densities are integrable by N002; integral linearity and scalar multiplication identify ∫Fseq(k) dμ=(E(t0+hseq(k))-E(t0))/hseq(k). Thus the energy difference quotients converge to ∫e_t(y,t0) dμ along this sequence.

Discharge L2 in F004 and quantify the arbitrary sequence. Any sequence of nonzero real increments tending to zero eventually satisfies |h|<η, so discarding its finite initial part yields the same limit. The sequential criterion for limits in R now gives the full two-sided difference-quotient limit at zero. Explicitly, if that limit failed, a fixed positive error could be attained by nonzero increments arbitrarily close to zero; choosing one at distance less than min(η,1/(k+1)) for each k would contradict the just-proved sequence limit. Thus E is differentiable at t0 and E'(t0)=∫ e_t(x,t0) dx. Substitute F001 and use finite linearity of the integral; every summand is absolutely integrable by N002. This yields E'(t0)=2∫u_t·u_tt dx+2∑_{j=1}^n ∫∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t dx, at time t0. The pointwise formula, finiteness, and arbitrary choice of t0 prove all asserted differentiation identities and finiteness clauses.

Fix t0>0 and j∈{1,…,n}; H001 supplies n≥1. Choose C,R from N002 for J=[t0/2,3t0/2], and set Q=[-R,R]^n. Define g(x)=u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0). By H002 it is smooth. Its derivative, by the product rule, is ∂_{x_j}g=∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u+u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u at time t0. By N002, both summands, g and its derivative are integrable and vanish off C. Since C⊂int(Q), the complement of C is an open neighborhood of the boundary of Q, and g vanishes there. In particular the two j-coordinate face values are zero.

Use the coordinate insertion I_j(y,z), with coordinate j equal to z and remaining coordinates given by y. Fix arbitrary y∈[-R,R]^(n-1), and define fline(z)=g(I_j(y,z)), dline(z)=∂_{x_j}g(I_j(y,z)). By F001 and the coordinate chain rule, fline is smooth, its derivative is dline, and both endpoint values fline(-R),fline(R) are zero. The continuous derivative dline is bounded and integrable on [-R,R]. Apply M003 with real codomain and a=-R,b=R: ∫_{-R..R}dline(z) dz=fline(R)-fline(-R)=0. Endpoints are null for one-dimensional Lebesgue measure, so the same holds for the integral over [-R,R]. Since y was arbitrary, the integral in coordinate j of ∂_{x_j}g is zero for every choice of remaining box coordinates.

Set v(y,z)=∂_{x_j}g(I_j(y,z)). Split Q into its remaining n-1 coordinates and coordinate j, with their restricted Lebesgue measures. This is the same measure as μ restricted to Q under I_j: on every coordinate subrectangle both give the product of its side lengths, and these rectangles determine the finite measures; the coordinate reordering merely reorders these factors. Both restricted measures are finite, hence s-finite. The function v is continuous and bounded on the compact product box, so it is integrable for that finite product measure. Apply M004 to v with the remaining coordinates as the outer variable and coordinate j as the inner variable. This gives ∫_Q ∂_{x_j}g dx=∫_{[-R,R]^(n-1)}(∫_{[-R,R]}∂_{x_j}g(I_j(y,z)) dz) dy=0 by F002. For n=1 the remaining-coordinate space is R^0, a singleton with its zero-dimensional Lebesgue measure of mass one, so the identical formula reduces to the one-dimensional integral; no exceptional empty-coordinate case is omitted.

By F001 all terms vanish off C⊂Q, so F003 gives ∫_{R^n}∂_{x_j}g dx=0. The product identity in F001 and integral linearity, justified by absolute integrability of both summands, give 0=∫_{R^n} ∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0) dx+∫_{R^n}u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_jx_j}u(x,t0) dx. Symmetry of the dot product and rearrangement yield ∫∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t dx=-∫u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx, with all terms at time t0. Quantify over the arbitrary t0 and j to conclude the asserted integration-by-parts formula and its finiteness assertions.

Fix arbitrary t0>0. H001 gives finitely many spatial coordinates, and H002 supplies the derivative notation. N002 proves e(·,t0) integrable and thereby makes the guarded definition of E available. N003 proves differentiability of E at t0 and the absolutely finite identity E'(t0)=2∫u_t·u_tt dx+2∑_{j=1}^n∫∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t dx. Apply N004 at t0 for each of the finitely many spatial indices to replace each second integral by -∫u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx.

By the definition Δ_xu=∑_{j=1}^n∂_{x_jx_j}u and finite linearity of these integrable terms, F001 becomes E'(t0)=2∫_{R^n}u_t(x,t0)·(u_tt(x,t0)-Δ_xu(x,t0)) dx. N001 states that this integrand is zero pointwise, hence E'(t0)=0. Since t0 was arbitrary, E is differentiable on (0,∞) and has zero derivative at every positive time. N002 already supplies integrability for every such time.

For completeness take any 0<a0<b0. F002 gives differentiability, hence continuity, of E at all points of [a0,b0], and derivative zero on (a0,b0). Apply M002 with f equal to E on positive times, derivative function zero there, and endpoints a0,b0 (extend f arbitrarily to nonpositive arguments). It yields (E(b0)-E(a0))/(b0-a0)=0; since b0-a0>0, E(b0)=E(a0). Equality is automatic for coincident times, and for reversed positive times interchange their roles. Therefore E is constant on (0,∞). Together with F002 and the definition of E this proves the complete conclusion with coefficient one on both squared norms and without any time-zero assertion.

460: /-- A function is continuously differentiable up to `n` on `s` if, for any point `x` in `s`, it
461: admits continuous derivatives up to order `n` on a neighborhood of `x` in `s`.
462: The parameter `n` belongs to `ℕ∞ω` (accessible in the `ContDiff` scope), i.e. it can be a natural
463: number, `∞`, or `ω`.
464: 
465: For `n = ∞`, we only require that this holds up to any finite order (where the neighborhood may
466: depend on the finite order we consider).
467: For `n = ω`, we require the function to be analytic within `s` at every point of `s`. The precise
468: definition we give (all the derivatives should be analytic) is more involved to work around issues
469: when the space is not complete, but it is equivalent when the space is complete.
470: -/

import Mathlib
open scoped BigOperators ContDiff
open MeasureTheory Set Filter
namespace WaveEnergy
abbrev X (n : ℕ) := Fin n → ℝ
abbrev V (m : ℕ) := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin m)
def domain (n : ℕ) : Set (X n × ℝ) := {p | 0 < p.2}
noncomputable def mu (n : ℕ) : Measure (X n) := Measure.pi (fun _ : Fin n => (volume : Measure ℝ))
noncomputable def dt {n : ℕ} {F : Type} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F]
    (f : X n × ℝ → F) (p : X n × ℝ) : F := deriv (fun r : ℝ => f (p.1, r)) p.2
noncomputable def dx {n : ℕ} {F : Type} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F]
    (f : X n × ℝ → F) (j : Fin n) (p : X n × ℝ) : F :=
  fderiv ℝ (fun y : X n => f (y, p.2)) p.1 (Pi.single j 1)
noncomputable def lap {n m : ℕ} (u : X n × ℝ → V m) (p : X n × ℝ) : V m :=
  ∑ j : Fin n, dx (dx u j) j p
noncomputable def density {n m : ℕ} (u : X n × ℝ → V m) (p : X n × ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ‖dt u p‖ ^ 2 + ∑ j : Fin n, ‖dx u j p‖ ^ 2
noncomputable def energy {n m : ℕ} (u : X n × ℝ → V m) (t : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∫ x : X n, density u (x, t) ∂mu n
noncomputable def kinetic {n m : ℕ} (u : X n × ℝ → V m) (p : X n × ℝ) : ℝ :=
  inner ℝ (dt u p) (dt (dt u) p)
noncomputable def mixed {n m : ℕ} (u : X n × ℝ → V m) (j : Fin n) (p : X n × ℝ) : ℝ :=
  inner ℝ (dx u j p) (dx (dt u) j p)
noncomputable def lapTerm {n m : ℕ} (u : X n × ℝ → V m) (j : Fin n) (p : X n × ℝ) : ℝ :=
  inner ℝ (dt u p) (dx (dx u j) j p)
noncomputable def flux {n m : ℕ} (u : X n × ℝ → V m) (j : Fin n) (p : X n × ℝ) : ℝ :=
  inner ℝ (dt u p) (dx u j p)
def box {n : ℕ} (R : ℝ) : Set (X n) := {x | ∀ j, x j ∈ Icc (-R) R}
def scalarTerms {n m : ℕ} (u : X n × ℝ → V m) : Set (X n × ℝ → ℝ) :=
  {f | f = density u ∨ f = dt (density u) ∨ f = kinetic u ∨
    ∃ j : Fin n, f = mixed u j ∨ f = lapTerm u j ∨ f = flux u j ∨ f = dx (flux u j) j}
structure Window {n m : ℕ} (u : X n × ℝ → V m) (q : V m)
    (t0 : ℝ) (C : Set (X n)) (R : ℝ) : Prop where
  compact : IsCompact C
  radius_pos : 0 < R
  inside : ∀ x ∈ C, ∀ j : Fin n, x j ∈ Ioo (-R) R
  constant : ∀ x, x ∉ C → ∀ r ∈ Icc (t0 / 2) (3 * t0 / 2), u (x, r) = q
  box_volume : mu n (box R) = ENNReal.ofReal ((2 * R) ^ n)
  box_finite : mu n (box R) < ⊤
  derivatives_zero : ∀ k : ℕ, 0 < k → ∀ x, x ∉ C →
    ∀ r ∈ Ioo (t0 / 2) (3 * t0 / 2), iteratedFDeriv ℝ k u (x, r) = 0
  sections : ∀ f ∈ scalarTerms u, ∀ r ∈ Ioo (t0 / 2) (3 * t0 / 2),
    Continuous (fun x => f (x, r)) ∧ (∀ x, x ∉ C → f (x, r) = 0) ∧
    Integrable (fun x => f (x, r)) (mu n)
  uniform : ∀ f ∈ scalarTerms u, ∀ a b : ℝ,
    Icc a b ⊆ Ioo (t0 / 2) (3 * t0 / 2) →
    ∃ B : ℝ, 0 ≤ B ∧ ∀ x ∈ box R, ∀ r ∈ Icc a b, |f (x, r)| ≤ B
end WaveEnergy
open WaveEnergy

All finite-dimensional coordinate norms give the same smooth structure. import Mathlib

open MeasureTheory Set Filter
namespace WaveEnergy
abbrev X (n : ℕ) := Fin n → ℝ
abbrev V (m : ℕ) := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin m)
def domain (n : ℕ) : Set (X n × ℝ) := {p | 0 < p.2}
noncomputable def mu (n : ℕ) : Measure (X n) := Measure.pi (fun _ : Fin n => (volume : Measure ℝ))
noncomputable def dt {n : ℕ} {F : Type} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F]
    (f : X n × ℝ → F) (p : X n × ℝ) : F := deriv (fun r : ℝ => f (p.1, r)) p.2
noncomputable def dx {n : ℕ} {F : Type} [NormedAddCommGroup F] [NormedSpace ℝ F]
    (f : X n × ℝ → F) (j : Fin n) (p : X n × ℝ) : F :=
  fderiv ℝ (fun y : X n => f (y, p.2)) p.1 (Pi.single j 1)
noncomputable def lap {n m : ℕ} (u : X n × ℝ → V m) (p : X n × ℝ) : V m :=
  ∑ j : Fin n, dx (dx u j) j p
noncomputable def density {n m : ℕ} (u : X n × ℝ → V m) (p : X n × ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ‖dt u p‖ ^ 2 + ∑ j : Fin n, ‖dx u j p‖ ^ 2
noncomputable def energy {n m : ℕ} (u : X n × ℝ → V m) (t : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∫ x : X n, density u (x, t) ∂mu n
noncomputable def kinetic {n m : ℕ} (u : X n × ℝ → V m) (p : X n × ℝ) : ℝ :=
  inner ℝ (dt u p) (dt (dt u) p)
noncomputable def mixed {n m : ℕ} (u : X n × ℝ → V m) (j : Fin n) (p : X n × ℝ) : ℝ :=
  inner ℝ (dx u j p) (dx (dt u) j p)
noncomputable def lapTerm {n m : ℕ} (u : X n × ℝ → V m) (j : Fin n) (p : X n × ℝ) : ℝ :=
  inner ℝ (dt u p) (dx (dx u j) j p)
noncomputable def flux {n m : ℕ} (u : X n × ℝ → V m) (j : Fin n) (p : X n × ℝ) : ℝ :=
  inner ℝ (dt u p) (dx u j p)
def box {n : ℕ} (R : ℝ) : Set (X n) := {x | ∀ j, x j ∈ Icc (-R) R}
def scalarTerms {n m : ℕ} (u : X n × ℝ → V m) : Set (X n × ℝ → ℝ) :=
  {f | f = density u ∨ f = dt (density u) ∨ f = kinetic u ∨
    ∃ j : Fin n, f = mixed u j ∨ f = lapTerm u j ∨ f = flux u j ∨ f = dx (flux u j) j}
structure Window {n m : ℕ} (u : X n × ℝ → V m) (q : V m)
    (t0 : ℝ) (C : Set (X n)) (R : ℝ) : Prop where
  compact : IsCompact C
  radius_pos : 0 < R
  inside : ∀ x ∈ C, ∀ j : Fin n, x j ∈ Ioo (-R) R
  constant : ∀ x, x ∉ C → ∀ r ∈ Icc (t0 / 2) (3 * t0 / 2), u (x, r) = q
  box_volume : mu n (box R) = ENNReal.ofReal ((2 * R) ^ n)
  box_finite : mu n (box R) < ⊤
  derivatives_zero : ∀ k : ℕ, 0 < k → ∀ x, x ∉ C →
    ∀ r ∈ Ioo (t0 / 2) (3 * t0 / 2), iteratedFDeriv ℝ k u (x, r) = 0
  sections : ∀ f ∈ scalarTerms u, ∀ r ∈ Ioo (t0 / 2) (3 * t0 / 2),
    Continuous (fun x => f (x, r)) ∧ (∀ x, x ∉ C → f (x, r) = 0) ∧
    Integrable (fun x => f (x, r)) (mu n)
  uniform : ∀ f ∈ scalarTerms u, ∀ a b : ℝ,
    Icc a b ⊆ Ioo (t0 / 2) (3 * t0 / 2) →
    ∃ B : ℝ, 0 ≤ B ∧ ∀ x ∈ box R, ∀ r ∈ Icc a b, |f (x, r)| ≤ B
abbrev Other (n : ℕ) (j : Fin n) := {i : Fin n // i ≠ j} → ℝ
noncomputable def otherMu {n : ℕ} (j : Fin n) : Measure (Other n j) :=
  Measure.pi (fun _ : {i : Fin n // i ≠ j} => (volume : Measure ℝ))
def otherBox {n : ℕ} (j : Fin n) (R : ℝ) : Set (Other n j) :=
  {y | ∀ i, y i ∈ Icc (-R) R}
def insert {n : ℕ} (j : Fin n) (p : Other n j × ℝ) : X n :=
  fun i => if h : i = j then p.2 else p.1 ⟨i,h⟩
end WaveEnergy
